title: Operate and Secure Persistence
readerIntent: Secure, monitor, tune, recover, and qualify persistence.
priorKnowledge: Know the data topology and selected provider.
owner: Deployment operators and selected database provider
summary: Production persistence needs provider-qualified encryption, credentials, capacity, indexing, backup, recovery, failover, and tenant isolation.

sections.heading: Secure
items: Use authenticated encrypted connections and least-privilege credentials.
Keep secrets in governed secret layers and rotate them safely.
Enforce schema read/write and field policy before provider calls.
Prevent cross-tenant connection, model, cache, log, and backup leakage.

sections.heading: Monitor
items: Connection and pool health, saturation, wait time, and reconnects.
Operation latency, throughput, conflicts, timeouts, and errors.
Slow queries, scans, index use, storage growth, and transaction outcomes.
Tenant-safe dimensions, backup freshness, replication lag, and restore evidence.

sections.heading: Recover and qualify
items: Test startup without the provider and mid-operation outage.
Prove reconnect, retry limits, idempotency, transaction rollback, and cleanup.
Exercise backup, point-in-time or supported restore, failover, schema migration, rollback, and version upgrade.
Load-test realistic query shapes and isolation; a local happy-path test is insufficient.

sections.heading: Security baseline
items: Use separate least-privilege identities for applications, migrations, backup, and administration.
Require encrypted transport and provider-appropriate encryption at rest.
Restrict network reachability to approved runtime and operator paths.
Rotate secrets without committing or logging them.
Audit administrative and sensitive data operations.
Apply retention, deletion, privacy, and regulatory controls to data and backups.

sections.heading: Capacity and performance
items: Measure representative read, write, update, relationship, bulk, and transaction workloads.
Size connection pools against process count and provider limits.
Inspect query plans and indexes before scaling hardware.
Set operation deadlines and bound result sizes.
Monitor storage, memory, CPU, I/O, replication, and growth.
Run load and soak tests with tenant isolation and expected concurrency.

sections.heading: Backup and restore
paragraphs: A completed backup job is not recovery evidence. Define recovery-point and recovery-time objectives, retention, encryption, access, off-site or regional placement, and restore ownership.
Restore into an isolated environment regularly, validate schemas, indexes, tenants, record counts, application reads, search/cache rebuilds, and audit the exercise.

sections.heading: Migration and upgrade
items: Inventory provider, driver, server, schema, index, and topology compatibility.
Back up and prove rollback before destructive changes.
Test migrations using production-representative volume.
Coordinate staged and online systems plus import/export and search projections.
Observe error, latency, conflict, and replication signals after rollout.
Keep a time-bounded rollback decision and accountable owner.

sections.heading: Incident examples
items: Pool exhaustion: reject or queue within bounds, identify leaks or slow queries, and avoid unlimited pool growth.
Provider outage: change readiness, stop unsafe retries, preserve idempotency, and communicate degraded behavior.
Slow query: capture safe shape and plan, add or adjust an owned index, then regression-test writes.
Tenant-routing error: stop affected operations, preserve evidence, assess exposure, correct mapping, and reconcile.
Restore required: follow the verified runbook and rebuild derived cache/search state.

sections.heading: Production readiness evidence
items: Current supported-version matrix and provider maturity.
Threat model, network, credential, encryption, and audit review.
Load, soak, outage, reconnect, failover, and recovery tests.
Recent successful restore and migration rollback exercise.
Dashboards, alerts, runbooks, on-call ownership, and escalation.
Known limits, capacity headroom, and scheduled requalification.
